prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B056, Katori and Ye, as the sole prize part. After the full exchange my confidence has grown, and the reason is the quality of the evidence more than the vote count. Every member ranked it, the same two names were proposed by all eight, and the five members who prefer it argue from independent confirmation, which is the test I apply to any instrument result. The magic-wavelength condition lets a very large number of neutral atoms be interrogated with Doppler, recoil and net light-shift effects removed. That is the mechanism that took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18, and it has been reproduced and surpassed at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE. It has also produced physics and not only a better clock: gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, tighter limits on variation of constants, searches for dark-matter couplings, and many-body effects in the clock itself. Katori supplied the concept and first demonstrations, and Ye took it to the accuracy and stability frontier. I take Danielsson's and Kroll's point that the case should rest on this physics, so the citation should name the invention and the 1e-18 performance it enabled, not just the instrument.
statement.case_against: The chair's questions in my own summary remain the real weaknesses. First, the lattice clock builds on the comb (2005) and ion control and cooling (2012 and 1997), so the citation must present it as a distinct invention. Second, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Sterr, Schmidt and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams made decisive contributions that two names cannot hold, and the Al+ and ion-clock line is a parallel path that a sceptic will cite. Third, Danielsson is right that this is strictly an invention and measurement capability, not the discovery of a new phenomenon; I think the redshift, constants and dark-matter results answer this only in part. Fourth, the redefinition of the second has not happened. I am not an atomic physicist and rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the fine points of the physics and the attribution.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the clock and not a precondition for recognising it, since the 1e-18 performance and its reproduction in several laboratories are already in place. She also says the atomic structure and light-shift theory are well understood, so theory and experiment agree.
responses.response: This is the argument that settles the timing question for me. In round 1 I treated waiting for the redefinition as a point that could be argued. I now regard it as a reason neither for nor against, because the evidence we judge is the demonstrated performance and its independent reproduction, not a decision by metrology bodies. I would ask her, as the atomic physicist, to state whether Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration, and Ye's accuracy and many-body results, are separable enough in the record that the two-name credit is fair and does not pass over Takamoto or Lemonde as co-originators.

responses.point: Kroll names the parallel strontium-clock work (Lemonde at SYRTE, Sterr and Schmidt at PTB, Takamoto and Katori in Tokyo, Ludlow and Bloom at NIST and JILA) and says Ye's best results use comb and laser-stabilisation technology the 2005 prize already honoured. He still judges the credit chain short and defensible, and judges waiting for the redefinition unnecessary.
responses.response: I agree with his judgement on timing and accept his account of the overlap, which is the sharpest statement of the case against. My answer to the comb overlap is that the 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool and the lattice clock is a different step: a neutral-atom trap in which the trap itself drops out of the measurement. Takamoto and Katori are in the same Tokyo group, so that parallel line is partly inside Katori's credit. The citation should say 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock', which honours the idea without claiming that no other group built a strontium clock. I would welcome his reading of whether Ye's use of the comb makes the citation read as a continuation of 2005.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new class of quantum matter with fifteen years of independent confirmation, calls the claim arguably overdue, and defers to the atomic physicists on whether the clock is a discovery or a measurement capability.
responses.response: B007 remains my first alternative and I think it is the deepest conceptual candidate on the list, so I do not take his preference lightly. I still would not move it above B056 for three reasons. The credit gap around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a real weakness he names himself, and the late Shoucheng Zhang's position makes a trio harder to defend. The 2016 prize on topological matter gives a critic a ready argument, as Mehlig also notes. And the criterion for choosing between two sound candidates should be credit clarity, since breadth of support is a weaker guide than the scientific record. On that criterion B056 is ahead. If B007 is raised again next year, I would want the citation question settled first.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B007 as a distinct, experimentally anchored achievement and asks me to say concretely what Halzen and Karle did that others did not, since AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal and the collaboration-wide analysis make a two-name IceCube credit contestable.
responses.response: I owe a concrete answer. Halzen was the intellectual driver of the cubic-kilometre concept and the case for it, and Karle led the detector construction, the ice-optics and calibration programme that made the detector work. The first is the idea and the second is the instrument. That is a credible pair in my own field, but it is not an uncontested one, because the AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers and the very large collaboration that produced the 2013 result are not covered, and I cannot claim that two names are a complete account. With the source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) still at evidence level, I now accept that B003 is an alternative for a later year and not my first choice.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from EHT to the clock and says plainly that the clock is strictly an invention and measurement capability, resting on combs and laser cooling, with the physics in applications that have not yet delivered a surprise. He also asks whether IceCube attribution can be settled for this year.
responses.response: On IceCube I answer no: I do not think the attribution can be settled for this year, for the reasons I give to Mehlig, and it would be wrong of me to push it as chair because it is my field. On his invention-versus-discovery point I mostly agree and I do not think the committee should hide it. The lattice clock is a measurement capability, and the justification for it is that it works as an instrument of discovery: a probe of redshift, constants and dark-matter couplings whose results are real even where they have so far shown agreement with expectation. A null result at 1e-18 is a measurement of nature, but I accept that this is a judgement call that some members will weigh differently.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B032 and asks whether B056 is stronger than she allowed, while asking the committee to consider whether she should recuse herself on B032 and noting the thin opening support and the Nion line as weaknesses of her own choice.
responses.response: I think she has judged it correctly: B056 has the broader support and the shorter credit chain, and she has already ranked it as her first alternative. I take her point about the Wolf Prize and agree that it does not count as merit on its own; it is a sign the community agrees on the credit, not proof of priority. Her disclosure of closeness to the TEM field is the right course, and I would suggest that she abstain on B032 if it comes to a vote. It does not bear on B056, so her view on the clock carries full weight.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct invention when the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize lie underneath it.
Whether Katori and Ye is the fairest pair given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Sterr, Schmidt and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups.
Whether a few more years would bring a decisive result, such as a redefinition of the second or a significant dark-matter or constants bound, that would make the discovery element clearer.
Whether B007 should have priority, which depends on whether the committee can settle the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit.
Whether IceCube source identification will mature in the next few years, since I now see B003 as a later-year candidate.
statement.conflict_note: I have no specific link to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. I am not an atomic physicist and rely on Lindroth and Kroll on B056. I am not an IceCube member, but IceCube is in my own field, and I have therefore taken extra care not to push B003. I belong to the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, none of which bears on any shortlisted candidate. As chair I am moving this stage forward and not seeking to impose consensus.
